cards.title: AI Code Is Fast, But Is It *Right*? The Next Big Opportunity Is Trust.
cards.thesis: AI tools are amazing for quickly generating code, but developers are realizing it's super hard to tell if that code is actually correct, up-to-date, or pulling from legitimate sources. This lack of trust is slowing people down, making them question their own skills, and highlighting a huge gap in the current AI ecosystem.

evidence.text: One developer shared that 'Coding Agents killed my identity,' feeling that programming is like a game they no longer enjoy winning if an AI engine plays for them.
A common question is 'How do you review and validate LLM generated code?' because models often give different 'findings' and it's hard to filter through the noise to find real defects.

A user noted that when working with an LLM like Qwen3.8, instead of fetching expected documentation URLs, it tried fetching 'weird URLs' like random proxy links, showing issues with source reliability.
People are asking 'Are you good at AI, or just using it?' and trying to define proficiency levels, from simple prompt-and-response to orchestrating multiple AI agents, highlighting a new skill gap.
The OpenCode harness, a tool for using various free AI models, recently stopped including DeepSeek, showing how quickly available AI models and their capabilities can change.

cards.opportunity: Developers are drowning in AI-generated code they can't trust, constantly second-guessing if it's outdated or pulling from sketchy sources like 'weird URLs' a model spit out. The immediate win is a lightweight tool, maybe an IDE plugin or browser extension, that acts as an AI 'code fact-checker' by automatically verifying generated snippets against known, up-to-date official documentation or common library versions. Ship a first version that flags potentially stale or incorrect API calls for popular frameworks, and you'll own the frustrated developer market, giving them back their confidence to actually ship AI-assisted products.

cards.title: Gamers Are Obsessed With Gaining an Edge: The Hidden Opportunity in the 'Cheat' Economy
cards.thesis: Competitive gamers are always looking for an advantage, and developers are actively building and sharing tools like 'no recoil' macros (software that eliminates weapon kickback) and 'aimbots' (software that automatically targets enemies) for popular titles like Apex Legends. This isn't just a niche; the demand is strong enough that people are creating and updating these projects for years into the future.

evidence.text: A GitHub project offering an Apex Legends 'no recoil' macro for multiple weapons, including the R-301, Flatline, and Hemlok, saw 21 engagements.
Another GitHub project, an external aimbot for Apex Legends with features like lock-on, hitbox selection, and prediction, garnered 19 engagements.

cards.opportunity: Competitive gamers are constantly hunting for an edge, and public GitHub repos for Apex Legends 'no recoil' macros and 'aimbots' (tools to improve aiming) show this demand is strong and ongoing, even looking ahead to '2026'. But the biggest fear is getting banned or installing malware. Instead of building the cheat, you could own the trust layer: set up a dead-simple review site or curated forum that focuses purely on vetting these kinds of game enhancement tools for safety, effectiveness, and ban-risk, starting with open-source projects. You'd be solving a massive trust problem for thousands of gamers and could monetize through premium reviews or community access.

cards.title: Your AI Agent is Ready. Is it Fast Enough? Is it Even Deployed?
cards.thesis: While everyone's hyping up building new AI agents, the real headaches for companies are actually getting those agents to work seamlessly within their existing systems (integration) and making sure they run super fast (performance). This creates a massive demand for tools and services that simplify AI deployment and optimization, especially for folks who aren't deep into infrastructure.

evidence.text: SalesPatriot (a new YC startup from the Winter 2025 batch) is hiring 'Forward Deployed Engineers,' which means they need experts to help customers integrate their product directly into their specific company setups.

LiteLLM (a YC startup from the Winter 2023 batch), which helps developers connect to various AI models easily, is hiring 'Rust / Performance Engineers,' showing a clear focus on making AI interactions incredibly fast and efficient.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's building AI agents, but the silent killer is getting them deployed into actual business workflows and making them run fast enough to be useful. Instead of hiring expensive 'forward-deployed engineers,' small businesses desperately need a plug-and-play solution that lets non-technical teams connect their AI agents to existing tools (like Slack, Salesforce, etc.) and easily monitor/optimize their performance. You could build a simple dashboard that provides this 'virtual integration expert' service, allowing anyone to ship and tune their AI apps in a weekend.
